analysis.one_liner: Barred the futures regulator from issuing rules on swaps and hybrid derivatives contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote; it had three Republican sponsors and no recorded floor action before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the agency that oversees futures markets — from proposing or issuing any rule, interpretation, or policy statement that restricts or regulates swap agreements and qualifying hybrid instruments until September 30, 1999, or until Congress passed legislation funding the agency beyond fiscal year 2000, whichever came first. It would have frozen the legal status of these contracts as of January 1, 1998, locking in the exemptions the agency had granted since 1989. It kept the agency's enforcement powers, its ability to act in a market emergency, and its authority over agricultural trade options. The bill was a response to the agency's May 1998 'concept release' examining whether the fast-growing over-the-counter derivatives market needed new oversight.
analysis.who_benefits: Major banks and other dealers in the over-the-counter swaps market. Those contracts were already largely exempt under the agency's own safe harbors; the bill would have locked in those exemptions and barred the regulator from reconsidering them, shielding a market that industry argued might otherwise face 'legal uncertainty' and move offshore.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Major banks and OTC swaps dealers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibited the CFTC from proposing or issuing any rule or regulation that restricts or regulates qualifying hybrid instruments or swap agreements during the restraint period

Froze the legal status of these contracts as it existed between July 21, 1989 and January 1, 1998, and stated that the agency's February 1998 comment letter and May 1998 concept release on over-the-counter derivatives could not change that status
Preserved existing exemptions, including the CFTC's 1989 swap policy statement and 1990 hybrid-instrument interpretation, as the baseline the regulator could not revisit

Kept the agency's power to bring enforcement actions, respond to market emergencies, and act on agricultural trade options, which supporters could point to as evidence it was a pause rather than a ban on oversight

analysis.who_pays: Investors and counterparties dealing with an unregulated derivatives market, and ultimately the broader financial system and taxpayers, who backstop losses when large dealers fail. The bill tied the hands of the market's watchdog precisely while that market was expanding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors and taxpayers backing the financial system

drawbacks.text: The bill's own text acknowledges the trigger: the CFTC had just opened an examination (a 'concept release') of the over-the-counter derivatives market, and this bill declared that examination powerless to change anything — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge, since it blocked the one agency with futures-market jurisdiction from looking at a growing, largely unregulated market

Supporters argued, in the bill's 'reassurance' framing and in the broader debate of the time, that threatening the existing exemptions would create legal uncertainty and push the swaps business out of the United States; the bill tried to answer that by freezing the rules rather than by studying the risks the agency had raised

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered dealers continuity in a huge market and kept the agency's emergency and enforcement powers, so it was not an absolute ban on oversight. But its main effect was to tie the regulator's hands during the very period when it wanted to examine the market, and the broader approach it embodied — leave swaps alone — was enacted by Congress two years later and left that market essentially unregulated when derivatives helped drive the 2008 financial crisis. The savings to dealers came at the public's expense in risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House Agriculture subcommittee in late August 1998 and never acted on again before that Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Smith of Oregon, chair of the House Agriculture Committee, introduced the bill on August 6, 1998, joined by Reps. Combest and Ewing; it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture

The bill would have barred the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from proposing or issuing any rule, interpretation, or policy statement that restricts or regulates qualifying hybrid instruments or swap agreements until September 30, 1999, or until legislation was enacted authorizing the agency's funding for a fiscal year after 2000, whichever came first

It would have locked in the legal status of swaps and hybrid instruments as it stood on January 1, 1998, freezing the exemptions the agency had granted since 1989, and declared that the agency's May 1998 concept release on over-the-counter derivatives could not alter that status
It preserved the agency's enforcement authority, its power to respond to market emergencies, and its authority over agricultural trade options

On August 27, 1998 the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Risk Management and Specialty Crops; no markup, vote, or further action followed, and the 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999 with the bill dead

The deregulatory approach this bill embodied became law two years later: the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 barred the CFTC from regulating most swaps, leaving the over-the-counter derivatives market essentially unregulated on the eve of the 2008 financial crisis

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and swaps dealers were better off either way: the bill died without a vote, but their existing exemptions survived untouched, and two years later Congress enacted the broader version of this same deregulation.

for.name: Robert Smith of Oregon
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to bar the CFTC from regulating swaps and hybrid instruments

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on August 27, 1998, and took no further action before the Congress ended

against.name: Alan Greenspan, Robert Rubin, and Lawrence Summers
against.role: Federal Reserve Chair, Treasury Secretary, and Deputy Treasury Secretary
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed CFTC Chair Brooksley Born's push to regulate the over-the-counter derivatives market, backing the dealers' position that swaps needed no new rules

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.industry: Major banks and OTC derivatives dealers
industries.note: The bill would have locked in the exemptions that kept their swaps business outside the CFTC's reach and barred the regulator from revisiting them. Dealers gained by keeping a multi-trillion-dollar market away from oversight; the public carried the risk that the regulator had just begun to examine.

industries.industry: Corporate end users of swaps and hybrid instruments
industries.note: Companies using these contracts for hedging would have kept a familiar, unchanging legal framework. But their certainty came from the same freeze that blocked scrutiny of the market they were plugged into.

The agency's ability to write rules or even publish policy statements about swaps and hybrids would have been suspended during the restraint period. Its loss of authority was directly a loss of public protection.
